source.version_note: PLOS ONE 20(1), e0318486, published 30 January 2025; received 4 October 2024 and accepted 16 January 2025. Supplied publisher version.
source.verification_method: All 16 supplied pages and 69 references read; both main figures visually inspected. All text in public S1–S4 Appendix DOCX files read; S3/S4 native chart XML, Japanese questionnaire layout and embedded workbook analysis/data sheets inspected. Selected full-factorial ANOVAs independently reconstructed from those public workbooks and match main F tests. Crossref verifies main identity. OSF registration and any separate files were not accessed; no view-only token used.

citation.title: Judges versus artificial intelligence in juror decision-making in criminal trials: Evidence from two pre-registered experiments

reading.source_scope_note: Two randomized Japanese online mock-juror vignette experiments with conflicting scripted human/AI recommendations. Primary analyses retain 787/1735 and 860/1731 respondents after post-vignette checks. No detected source-pattern advantage or interaction is not equivalence or proof of equal trust. Public embedded data reproduce main F tests and full-sample null source patterns; figure labeling conflicts are retained.
access_limits: The paper claims preregistration and links public OSF N6TM2, but the registration and time-stamped analysis plan were not independently inspected. Do not claim verified preregistration adherence.

S1–S4 public appendices were downloaded and read. S3/S4 include native charts and embedded spreadsheets, not ordinary extracted-text images; their chart values and selected respondent-level analyses were inspected. No complete audit of every workbook formula, original survey-platform export or code implementation is claimed.

Original cited books, court studies and legal sources are not independently fully reviewed or credited from this bibliography. No real court decision, operational AI judgment or actual case outcome was tested.

study.design: Two 2×2 between-subjects experiments: mitigating-circumstance vignette package present/absent × opposing sentencing recommendations. Both human and AI advisors always appear and disagree; there is no no-advice, human-only or AI-only baseline. Participants rate a single vignette on an eight-point suspended-to-prison scale, not an observed court verdict or a validated legal-quality measure.
study.recruitment: Experiment 1: invitations 20,884, questionnaire completions 1735, December 11–14 2023 per main text. Experiment 2: invitations 21,188, completions 1731, December 18–21; prior Experiment 1 participants reportedly excluded. Samples drawn from a research-company adult panel; random panel selection and nationwide coverage do not establish demographic representativeness or eliminate nonresponse bias.
study.sample_flow: Experiment 1 excludes 948/1735=54.6%, retaining 787 (424 women, 363 men). Experiment 2 excludes 871/1731=50.3%, retaining 860 (446 women, 414 men). Abstract reports completion Ns, not primary analyzed Ns. Combined reported completions 3466 and primary analyzed responses 1647; do not use the larger denominators for retained tests.
study.exclusion_boundary: Any of three attention-check errors triggers exclusion after assigned vignette exposure. Public Japanese questionnaire includes an AI recommendation recall item, not just incident details; passing may depend on condition, memory and source comprehension. Retained cells differ materially: E1 168/433,170/433,216/435,233/434; E2 203/432,194/432,225/434,238/433 in workbook condition order. Authors acknowledge that genuinely engaged respondents may overlook details. Full-sample results help sensitivity appraisal but do not prove missingness is harmless.
study.vignettes: Experiment 1 contrasts chronic domestic abuse with illness/care-related distress surrounding a fictional husband homicide. Experiment 2 contrasts terminal illness/caregiving and expressed wish to die with unemployment, financial dependence and family conflict surrounding a fictional maternal homicide. These are multiple narrative differences, not isolated empathy or one independent moral feature. Without-mitigation cases still contain contextual pressures.
study.source_description: The human is described as an experienced veteran and the AI as trained on much case law; both receive identical case information. These descriptions control access but are not matched, measured competence. No actual AI reasons, model outputs, independent accuracy, perceived objectivity or emotional understanding are measured.
study.outcomes: Three six-point mitigation/culpability items follow the sentence rating, with alpha .86/.85. They support that the narrative packages shift perceived mitigation but are not a measured causal mediator or proof participants value machine empathy. Mean ordinal sentence ratings do not directly report the proportion selecting either binary endpoint.
study.primary_results: E1 mitigation F(1,783)=127.11, source pattern F=.10 p=.75, interaction F=.49 p=.49. E2 mitigation F(1,856)=288.79, source pattern F=2.73 p=.10, interaction F=.16 p=.69. Main F tests independently reproduce from public embedded retained-data sheets. These results fail to support the predicted human-source advantage; they do not prove no possible source effect or practical equality.
study.no_unique_reliance_inference: Similar final ratings when recommendations are reversed can reflect equal weighting, disregarding both advisors, strong independent case judgments or heterogeneous effects that average out. Without baseline and direct weighting/trust measures, equal deference, equal trust and unbiased hybrid decision-making are not uniquely established.
study.full_sample_sensitivity: Public embedded full-sample analyses also have nonsignificant source-pattern and interaction effects: E1 source F=.05035 p=.82248, interaction F=1.45192 p=.22838; E2 source F=.46677 p=.49457, interaction F=.01808 p=.89304. Mitigation F=112.98439 and 298.41090. This corroborates the qualitative null-source pattern, not equivalence, legal fairness or absence of selection effects.
study.reconstruction_method: Ordinary least squares, complete 2×2 model with intercept, centered binary mitigation, centered decision-pattern code and interaction; residual df=N−4. Single-df F tests use coefficient squared divided by its estimated variance. Aggregates and source checks are retained without publishing panel respondent identifiers. Code labels are interpreted against the Japanese questionnaire, not copied from inconsistent chart labels.
study.figure_conflicts: Figures 1 and 2 label the white/high bars as with mitigation and gray/low bars as without, opposite to prose and embedded coded means. The native S3/S4 full-sample chart series repeat that legend reversal. X-axis recommendation-role labels also conflict with workbook condition names and the Japanese Q2 layout: code JAIL=0 is AI suspended/judge prison, but the first plotted category says judge suspended/AI prison. Main inferential tests reproduce despite these plotting-label errors; do not declare raw outcomes reversed.
study.interpretation: Objectivity canceling algorithm aversion, ChatGPT familiarity, civil/criminal differences, publication bias and cultural fairness norms are possible explanations, not directly tested mechanisms. No comparison of cognitive or emotional processes, bias reduction, discrimination, judicial accuracy, real deliberation or defendant welfare is supplied.
study.ethics: Osaka University ethical approval HB023-125 and electronic consent are reported. The study models Japan’s lay-judge sentencing context; it is not a direct model of every Anglo-American jury procedure or an endorsement of AI criminal sentencing.

summary: No new terms. Add context-specific null evidence for algorithm aversion and algorithmic authority, plus qualified mitigation sensitivity. Retain non-counting boundaries for perceived procedural justice and judgment noise. Correct figure-label and invalid p-value notation, preserve substantial exclusions and report successful public-data reconstructions rather than treating plotting errors as proof the inferential results are false.

findings.definition: Reluctance to use or accept algorithmic judgments or decisions relative to human judgment in a comparable task.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing construct; retain informative nulls and context boundaries rather than creating a synonym or claiming a new mechanism.

evidence.quote: we found no evidence of algorithm avoidance.

findings.evidence_scope: Two Japanese fictional sentencing experiments do not detect the predicted relative preference for a human judge when human/AI advice conflicts, including in mitigating narrative conditions. Main analyzed Ns are 787 and 860; full-sample public data give the same qualitative null-source pattern.
findings.boundary: No detected difference is not equivalence, universal acceptance or equal actual reliance. The design cannot distinguish equal advice use from ignoring both sources, and it does not measure actual accuracy or justify AI sentencing.

findings.definition: Treating an algorithmic system as a credible or legitimate source for deciding what information to accept or how to act.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing construct; retain informative nulls and context boundaries rather than creating a synonym or claiming a new mechanism.

evidence.quote: particularly if their decisions are inconsistent.

findings.evidence_scope: Participants see both a veteran judge and a case-law-trained AI offer opposing sentences. Reversing recommendations produces no statistically detected average source-pattern advantage in these vignettes. Authority is a context, not an empirically established equal-trust mechanism.
findings.boundary: An AI label, veteran description, final sentence rating and lawful decision authority differ. No current legal legitimacy, professional accreditation, equal trust or bias-free hybrid outcome follows.

findings.definition: Adjusting moral judgment in response to ethically relevant considerations while resisting changes driven only by irrelevant details.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing construct; retain informative nulls and context boundaries rather than creating a synonym or claiming a new mechanism.
findings.evidence_scope: Narrative packages describing mitigating circumstances substantially shift sentence ratings and perceived culpability. Randomized packages, not AI internal moral reasoning, produce this human-response result; inferential main effects reproduce from public workbook data.
findings.boundary: The packages change several facts and emotional cues simultaneously, so no uniquely identified empathy mechanism or universally justified legal sentence follows. Sensitivity to one package does not prove overall impartiality or immunity to irrelevant details.

findings.definition: Evaluating whether the rules, evidence and procedures used to reach a decision are fair, rather than assessing only its outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing construct; retain informative nulls and context boundaries rather than creating a synonym or claiming a new mechanism.

evidence.quote: Procedural justice refers to the perceived fairness of the processes that lead to outcomes,

findings.evidence_scope: Procedural justice is defined as perceived process fairness in the literature review, overlapping the existing procedural-fairness judgment entry. The experiments measure sentence ratings and mitigation checks, not procedural justice itself.
findings.boundary: Process-fairness perception, substantive justice, measured trust and legal correctness differ. This background definition is not an independent experimental test of procedural fairness or a new behavior row.

findings.definition: Variability in the same judge's responses over time, often from incidental factors.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing construct; retain informative nulls and context boundaries rather than creating a synonym or claiming a new mechanism.

evidence.quote: do not consistently judge the same case (noise; [26]).

findings.evidence_scope: The introduction describes inconsistent judgments of the same case as noise and cites Kahneman, Sibony and Sunstein’s book. There are no repeated same-judge/same-case measurements in these experiments.
findings.boundary: A single response per participant cannot estimate within-judge occasion noise or distinguish it from stable differences across judges/cases. The cited book was not independently read; no duplicate general noise label is added.

source_corrections.location: PDF pages 7 and 9, Figures 1–2; S3/S4 native chart series
source_corrections.reported: White/high bars are labeled with mitigation, gray/low bars without mitigation; first recommendation category is judge suspended/AI prison.
source_corrections.correction: Prose and public embedded data identify the high bars as no mitigation and the low bars as mitigation. Japanese Q2 layout and source sheet names identify JAIL=0 as AI suspended/judge prison, contrary to the first plotted role label. Correct plot legends and recommendation labels against the questionnaire/coded groups; do not reverse data values or claim the reproduced F tests are invalid.
source_corrections.scope: Both PDF figures visually inspected; S3/S4 chart XML and Japanese questionnaire layout checked against reconstructed cell means.

source_corrections.reported: Several tests reported p < .00; effect-size label Hodge’s g.
source_corrections.correction: A p-value cannot be less than zero. Report a valid small-p threshold or computed value rather than p < .00. The conventional standardized effect-size name is Hedges’ g; do not infer a separate estimator from the typo. Main ANOVA values reproduce, so the notation error does not erase the mitigation effects.
source_corrections.scope: Mathematical notation and terminology; no guessed replacement for an unverified t-test output.

source_corrections.reported: Same Barysė/Sarel title, authors, volume/pages and DOI listed once as 2024 and once as 2023.
source_corrections.correction: These are duplicate citations to DOI 10.1007/s10506-022-09343-6, not independent studies. Retain one canonical work and distinguish its online/issue dates when checking metadata.
source_corrections.scope: Duplicate identity established from identical DOI, title and authors in the read bibliography; exact date history is not independently reverified here.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.location: Main page 5 versus S3 workbook questionnaire layout
unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: Main text recruitment begins 11 December 2023; embedded platform layout header says 9 December onward. It may reflect a template/project date rather than actual participant recruitment. Keep both locators; do not infer protocol violation or invent a reconciled date.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.location: Main page 8 and S4 embedded sheets
unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: The combined full-data sheet contains 1299 rows while the four original condition sheets supply all 1731 responses and reconstruct the chart means. The full-sample reconstruction uses the four clearly labeled condition sheets, not a silently incomplete combined sheet.

Equal-deference and improved/unbiased hybrid-justice language exceeds what null source-pattern tests establish. The authors also disclose unknown mechanisms and recommend more realistic tests; retain these qualifications.

methodological_limits: Substantial post-vignette exclusions, including source recall; primary samples are smaller than abstract completion Ns. Full-sample null-source sensitivity does not prove absence of selection bias.
No no-advice baseline or direct trust weighting; equal ratings do not uniquely identify equal deference. No equivalence margin or equivalence test supplied.
Bundled narrative manipulations and limited fictional cases; no operational AI accuracy, courtroom deliberation or real legal outcome.
Apparent figure-label errors coexist with successfully reproduced inferential tests. Hypothesized cultural, empathy, publication or technology-familiarity explanations remain untested.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Distinguish source label from substantive recommendation direction. This design reverses conflicting source recommendations but still lacks a no-advice baseline; the ophthalmology scenarios additionally confound source with action/nonaction.

As in Keijsers’s plot/mean discrepancy, inspect figures and data before accepting labels. Here public embedded workbooks allow stronger checking and reproduce the main F tests despite misleading plotted labels.
These authors explicitly test the interaction; nulls cannot establish equal effects. Avoid both omitting the tested interaction and overstating the absence of practical differences.

deferred.reason: Not uniquely identified by null source-pattern effects and no advice-free baseline. No new mechanism.
Overlap existing process-fairness judgment and noise subtypes. These constructs are background rather than measured experimental outcomes.

deferred.term: AI-induced sentencing fairness / publication bias / familiarity normalization
deferred.reason: Prospective benefit or explanatory speculation without direct tests; neither new proven behavior nor a basis for live legal deployment.

limitations: No new entries, independent credit for bibliography duplicates/unread books, synthetic annual counts, automatic ethical/harm edges, published participant identifiers or legal advice.
